tagline: A glacier-carved road corridor links temple stone, silver mines and skiing towns.
intro: SR-210 climbs from Little Cottonwood Canyon’s mouth to Alta through a U-shaped valley carved by an alpine glacier. The Forest Service presents the scenic byway as a drive through a rugged, glacially carved corridor. In the lower canyon, smooth, steep rock faces rise several hundred feet. Visit Utah lists 15 minutes to Alta for its seven-mile byway description. Little Cottonwood Creek runs the canyon’s length from Cecret Lake at Alta westward. The watershed supplies drinking water to much of Salt Lake County.

The state legislature defined SR-210 in 1941, linking Wasatch Boulevard with the canyon road to Alta. In 1975, the Alta Bypass Road joined the route to provide an alternative when snow slides closed the main road. A proposed mountain connection to Brighton was included in the highway’s legal definition but never built; the route was formally cut back to Alta in 1994.

Begin at the canyon mouth, where pioneers quarried stone for the Salt Lake Temple. Granite Mountain stands one mile up the canyon. Continue to Snowbird, then farther up to Alta, the road’s terminus. Alta stands at 8,950 feet, among Utah’s highest cities. In Albion Basin, the canyon also contains rare and endemic plant species.
notice: The lower canyon’s smooth, steep rock faces include quartz monzonite, granite and granodiorite.

moments.title: Granite Mountain
moments.text: Granite Mountain’s name is less precise than its stone: the mass is primarily quartz monzonite. This igneous rock resembles granite in appearance and composition, and the same material went into the Salt Lake Temple and the facade of the LDS Conference Center. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints also excavated a records vault 600 feet into the canyon’s north side. Its controlled environment holds genealogical records; the church makes records available through Family History Centers and its FamilySearch website. Here, the mountain is both building material and a place for storing records.

moments.title: Snowbird
moments.text: The name Big Emma survives on a ski run in Snowbird’s Gad Valley, carrying a mining name into a different use of the canyon. Silver mining became a major local industry in the nineteenth century. Ted Johnson, a former manager of Alta Lodge, later explored the Peruvian Gulch and Emma Mine/Gad Valley watersheds below Alta as the setting for Snowbird. He partnered with Dick Bass in 1969, and the ski area opened in December 1971. The community now takes its identity from skiing and summer recreation on land once associated with mining.

moments.title: Alta
moments.text: Alta’s change from silver camp to ski town followed a fire, an avalanche and a long decline in mining. The fire struck in 1878 and the avalanche in 1885, destroying most of the original town. By the 1930s, George Watson was its only remaining resident. Facing back taxes on his mining claims, he donated much of his Alta land to the Forest Service with the condition that it become a ski area. Alf Engen was hired in 1935 to help develop it; Alta is now a town centered on the ski area.
